titleEn: X Spaces: Robert F. Kennedy Jr. — Reclaiming Democracy
titleZh: X Spaces：小罗伯特·F·肯尼迪——重拾民主
summaryEn: Musk hosted Democratic presidential candidate Robert F. Kennedy Jr. on a Twitter Space discussing free speech, public health, content moderation and his campaign.
summaryZh: 马斯克在一场 Twitter Space 中邀请民主党总统候选人小罗伯特·F·肯尼迪，讨论言论自由、公共卫生、内容审核及其竞选活动。

segments.textEn: All right, everybody, let's get started. Introduce our co hosts here, Bobby Kennedy Jr. And Elon. I'll start by introducing Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. I think everyone already knows he's a nephew of President John F. Kennedy. He's the son of Senator and Attorney General Robert F. Kennedy, who was assassinated after winning the California primary in the 1968 presidential election. Before entering presidential politics, RFK Jr.
segments.textZh: 好了，各位，我们开始吧。介绍一下这里的共同主持人，小鲍比·肯尼迪和埃隆。我先来介绍小罗伯特·F·肯尼迪。我想大家都已经知道，他是约翰·F·肯尼迪总统的侄子。他是参议员兼司法部长罗伯特·F·肯尼迪的儿子，后者在赢得 1968 年总统选举的加利福尼亚州初选后遭到刺杀。在进入总统政治领域之前，小罗伯特·F·肯尼迪。

segments.textEn: Was an environmental lawyer and activist in many areas. He was most famous for cleaning up the Hudson River. He was also outspoken on indigenous rights, peace, and civil liberties. He's also the founder of Children's Health Defense, a nonprofit that protects children from toxic chemical assault from pharmaceutical drugs and environmental pollution. So with that, Bobby and Elon, I think we're all excited to hear what you guys have to say.
segments.textZh: 曾是一名环境律师，并在许多领域从事活动。他最著名的事迹是清理哈德逊河。他也直言不讳地支持原住民权利、和平与公民自由。他还是儿童健康保护组织的创始人，该非营利组织保护儿童免受药物和环境污染造成的有毒化学物质侵害。那么接下来，鲍比和埃隆，我想我们都很期待听听你们要说些什么。

segments.textEn: Elon, a real pleasure meeting you and thank you so much for hosting us.
segments.textZh: 埃隆，很高兴见到你，非常感谢你主持我们的活动。

segments.textEn: You're most welcome. Thank you. This is a great opportunity for the public to hear directly from you and really looking forward to what you have to say.
segments.textZh: 非常欢迎。谢谢。这是一个让公众直接听到你讲话的绝佳机会，我非常期待听听你要说些什么。

segments.textEn: I also just want to thank you for your leadership on the. On just breaking this, the whole of the censorship. In fact, I say one thing, that Twitter was always kind of the last refuge for those of us who are trying to talk about issues that departed from the official orthodoxies that were being censored on the other platforms. And the first real effort at censorship happened in February 2019 when Adam Schiff sent a letter to all, to the heads of all the social media sites of Google, Facebook, now meta, Instagram, YouTube, Pinterest and others and demanding that they start censoring information about vaccines that didn't.
segments.textZh: 我还想感谢你在这件事上的领导。就是打破这一切，打破整个审查体系。事实上，我想说一点，对于我们这些试图讨论偏离官方正统观念、而这些讨论在其他平台上遭到审查的人来说，Twitter 一直算是最后的避难所。第一次真正的审查行动发生在 2019 年 2 月，当时亚当·希夫致函所有社交媒体网站的负责人，包括 Google、Facebook，也就是现在的 Meta、Instagram、YouTube、Pinterest 等，要求他们开始审查那些关于疫苗但并不。

segments.textEn: That was non compliant with the official narratives. And the only place, the only group that resisted Schiff at that time was ahead of the intelligence committee. So that was kind of the first indicator that the intelligence apparatus had an interest in public health. And the only one of the social media sites to resist those, those imprecations was, was Twitter. When Jack was running this and he, for some reason, he was able to say no to them when the rest of them weren't.
segments.textZh: 那些不符合官方叙事的信息。而唯一的地方、当时唯一抵制希夫的群体处在情报委员会之前。所以，这算是第一个迹象，表明情报机构对公共卫生有兴趣。在这些社交媒体网站中，唯一抵制那些、那些诅咒的是、是 Twitter。当时由杰克运营这个平台，而他、不知为何，他能够对他们说不，其他平台却不能。

segments.textEn: So I'm very happy. And your arrival at Twitter, Elon, has been, I think, a breath of fresh air for our country. You somehow understood, although you're from South Africa, you somehow under the tradition of free expression and how important that is to American democracy. So I'm very grateful to you.
segments.textZh: 所以我非常高兴。埃隆，我认为你来到 Twitter，为我们的国家带来了一股清新空气。尽管你来自南非，但你却不知为何处在自由表达的传统之下，以及这对美国民主有多么重要。所以我非常感谢你。

segments.textEn: You're most welcome. Yes, I think it's absolutely essential to have a robust democracy. We must have free speech. In the absence of that, democracy simply cannot function.
segments.textZh: 非常欢迎。是的，我认为要拥有强健的民主制度，言论自由绝对不可或缺。没有言论自由，民主根本无法运转。

segments.textEn: Yeah, it is free speech. And the free flow of information is the water, it's the sunlight, it's the fertilizer, it's the soil. Democracy. Without it, democracy withers and dies. There's never been a time in history when we look back and say that the people who are censoring free speech were the good guys. They're always the bad guys. They're always. It's always the first step toward totalitarianism. But also, you know, it's one of the things that the constitutional framers understood that totalitarian systems have a huge advantage over democracy because they're more efficient.
segments.textZh: 是的，就是言论自由。信息的自由流动就是水，就是阳光，就是肥料，就是土壤。民主。没有它，民主就会枯萎、死亡。历史上从来没有什么时候，我们回顾过去会说那些审查言论自由的人是好人。他们总是坏人。他们总是。这总是迈向极权主义的第一步。但同时，你知道，这也是宪法制定者所理解的事情之一：极权体制比民主体制拥有巨大优势，因为它们效率更高。

segments.textEn: Democracy is sloppy, it's slow. It advances two steps and retreats one step. It is the product of a lot of debate, which is slow moving and laborious. And the only advantage, the big advantage that we have over totalitarian systems is that the ideas that mature into policies are first annealed in a furnace of debate. And the best ideas then triumph in this marketplace of ideas, which does not happen at totalitarian system.
segments.textZh: 民主是杂乱的，也是缓慢的。它前进 2 步，再后退 1 步。它是大量辩论的产物，而辩论进展缓慢、过程艰苦。我们相对于极权体制唯一的优势，那个巨大优势，就是发展为政策的思想首先要在辩论的熔炉中经受锤炼。然后，最好的思想会在这个思想市场中胜出，而这种情况在极权体制中不会发生。

segments.textEn: And that's one of the things that the dynamics that the framers of our constitution understood that we would be able to out compete totalitarian systems and outlast them because of this dynamic that produced policies through debate and through discussion and conversation rather than through dictation.
segments.textZh: 这也是我们宪法的制定者所理解的动力之一：凭借这种通过辩论、讨论和对话，而不是通过命令来产生政策的动力，我们将能够在竞争中胜过极权体制，并比它们延续得更久。

segments.textEn: Absolutely. I couldn't agree more. The thing about democracies and free speech is that it's like washing your laundry in public. Yes, you see things that perhaps you know there's dirty laundry, but at least you see it. It's not hidden. And it's essential to have that debate, even if you disagree strongly with one side of the debate. If you don't allow such debates. The thing that I think people who are in favor of censorship really need to understand is that unless people that you don't like can say things that you don't like, it's not free speech.
segments.textZh: 完全正确。我完全赞同。民主和言论自由的特点是，它就像当众洗自己的衣服。是的，你会看到一些东西，也许你知道那里有脏衣服，但至少你能看到。它没有被隐藏起来。进行这种辩论至关重要，即使你强烈反对辩论中的一方。如果你不允许这种辩论。我认为支持审查的人真正需要明白的是，除非那些你不喜欢的人可以说你不喜欢的话，否则那就不是言论自由。

segments.textEn: And if you, if you start censoring, it's only a matter of time before that censorship is turned upon you.
segments.textZh: 而且，如果你、如果你开始审查，那么这种审查转而落到你头上只是时间问题。

segments.textEn: I mean, the First Amendment was written not for easy speech and likable speech and lovable people. It was written for hard times and to protect speech that nobody wants you to say. And I remember 977 when the Nazis wanted to march through Skokie, Illinois, which was a Jewish neighborhood. And the liberals of this country, the aclu, turned out in force to support that right, Even though they were appalled and disgusted by what the Nazis were saying and doing.
segments.textZh: 我的意思是，第一修正案不是为轻松的言论、讨人喜欢的言论和可爱的人而写的。它是为艰难时期而写的，也是为了保护那些没人希望你说出口的言论。我记得 977 年，纳粹分子想要在伊利诺伊州斯科基游行，那里是一个犹太人社区。这个国家的自由派人士和美国公民自由联盟大批出面支持那项权利，尽管他们对纳粹分子所说和所做的事情感到震惊和厌恶。

segments.textEn: Everybody agreed that we had to be willing to die for the right to do so. And that was the. That's the whole base of democracy, is that we allow people to talk about. And one of the things, you know, that. And one of the things that prompted me to run for president is what you were talking about is the end of transparency in our country. That government. There's so much going on now that it's done secretively, that where the decision making is opaque, where there are people who are.
segments.textZh: 所有人都同意，我们必须愿意为这样做的权利而死。而那是。那就是民主的全部基础，也就是我们允许人们谈论。而其中一件事，你知道，那个。促使我竞选总统的事情之一，正是你刚才谈到的我们国家透明度的终结。政府。现在有太多事情是在秘密进行的，决策过程不透明，有一些人正在。

segments.textEn: Who are making decisions, who are not necessarily elect officials at the public has fenced out. And so many Americans today feel like the promise of democracy has been a bait and switch and that we're no longer living in a democratic system where we are actually the sovereign of our own destinies, the sovereign, the deciders of our own faith, that people over whom we have no control, that money, interest, that large corporations have taken over.
segments.textZh: 正在作出决定的人，他们不一定是公众排斥在外的民选官员。如今有如此多的美国人觉得，民主的承诺是一场诱售骗局，我们已不再生活在一个真正由我们主宰自身命运、由我们主宰、决定自身信仰的民主制度中；那些我们无法控制的人、金钱、利益、大公司已经接管了一切。

segments.textEn: This kind of merger of state and corporate power that's happened in Washington, D.C. in the state capitals, has not only turned our regulatory agencies into predators against the American people, they're supposed to be our protectors, but also that all the decision making, the real decision making, has been taken from the American public. And that, you know, you see so many people. I'm in rural Pennsylvania today, and I'm surrounded by people who feel despair about our country, who are disillusioned, who are struggling with poverty for reasons that they don't understand, but they feel like they no longer are the masters of their own destiny.
segments.textZh: 这种发生在华盛顿特区和各州首府的国家权力与企业权力的合并，不仅让本应保护我们的监管机构变成了侵害美国人民的掠食者，还把所有决策、真正的决策都从美国公众手中夺走了。而且，你知道，你会看到如此多的人。我今天在宾夕法尼亚州乡村地区，周围都是对我们国家感到绝望的人，他们幻想破灭，因自己不理解的原因在贫困中挣扎，但他们觉得自己已不再是自身命运的主人。

segments.textEn: And I think a lot of that is because it's true. Our government has become an instrument of corporate power and it is not telling. And because of that, it has to lie to us. You know, it can't afford to be transparent because it actually told us what it was up to and why it was making certain decisions. People wouldn't put up with it. So everything has to be cloaked in fear and deception. And I think, you know, Americans, even though they don't understand it, they understand that something very wrong is happening to them.
segments.textZh: 而且我认为，其中很大一部分原因是，这确实是真的。我们的政府已经变成了企业权力的工具，而且它并没有如实相告。正因为如此，它不得不对我们撒谎。你知道，它承受不起透明公开，因为它真的告诉了我们它在做什么，以及为什么要作出某些决定。人们是不会容忍的。所以一切都必须笼罩在恐惧和欺骗之中。而且我认为，你知道，美国人即使并不理解这一点，也明白有非常不对劲的事情正在发生在他们身上。

segments.textEn: Absolutely. The thing actually I find truly bizarre and very different from the past is that it's not just large corporations and government that are in collusion, which has actually been the case for a while. I think it was Eisenhower that warned us about the military industrial conflict, for example, and he's someone who really knew about it. But the thing that I find difficult to forgive is that the legacy of traditional media is also almost entirely, with some exceptions, working in lockstep with the government and with.
segments.textZh: 完全正确。实际上，我觉得真正离奇、而且与过去非常不同的是，相互勾结的不只是大公司和政府，尽管这种情况实际上已经存在一段时间了。比如，我想是艾森豪威尔曾警告我们提防军工冲突，而他是真正了解这件事的人。但我觉得难以原谅的是，传统媒体的遗产也几乎完全在与政府步调一致地行事，虽有一些例外，以及与。

segments.textEn: With corporate America. And they. It is really their obligation to question the government, not to Go along with it and be their mouthpiece in the United States. This is insane.
segments.textZh: 与美国企业界一起。而他们。他们真正的义务是质疑政府，而不是在美国附和政府并充当其传声筒。这太疯狂了。

segments.textEn: I mean, the function of the media traditionally is supposed as the guardians of the First Amendment. They're supposed to speak truth to power. And instead they've become propaganda vessels for the powerful, for, you know, the big. The military industrial complex, for the pharmaceutical companies or and for other large corporations. You know, one of the mechanisms by which which that media capture has taken place is buying through advertising, and particularly in the pharmaceutical realm.
segments.textZh: 我的意思是，传统上，媒体的职能应该是充当第一修正案的守护者。它们应该向权力说真话。可它们反而成了权势者的宣传工具，为了，你知道，那些大。军工复合体、制药公司，或以及其他大公司。你知道，媒体被收编的机制之一，就是通过广告进行收买，尤其是在制药领域。

segments.textEn: In 1997, we changed the law in this country. We had always forbidden the use of the media to sell pharmaceutical products. There was no direct to consumer advert of pharmaceutical products. It was against the law. FDA changed that law in 97, and it launched a tsunami of pharmaceutical dollars into the advertising space and gave the pharmaceutical companies control not only of the platform for advertising their products, but also control of content.
segments.textZh: 1997年，我们修改了这个国家的法律。我们过去一直禁止利用媒体销售药品。过去没有直接面向消费者的药品广告。这是违法的。FDA在97年修改了那项法律，由此掀起了一场制药资金涌入广告领域的海啸，并让制药公司不仅控制了宣传其产品的平台，还控制了内容。

segments.textEn: On Nightly News, I had this weird meeting with Roger Ailes. Roger Aile, the founder of Fox News. And I had this very strange relationship with him because I spent three months in a tent with him in East Africa when I was 19 years old. And even if that was before he started Fox News, once he started Fox News, he became kind of this Darth Vader figure for me, despite the fact that all the things he was doing to our country were antithetical to what I believed.
segments.textZh: 在《晚间新闻》上，我和罗杰·艾尔斯有过一次奇怪的会面。罗杰·艾尔，福克斯新闻的创始人。我和他的关系非常奇特，因为我19岁时曾在东非和他一起住在帐篷里3个月。即使那是在他创办福克斯新闻之前，但他一创办福克斯新闻，就成了我眼中某种达斯·维德式的人物，尽管他对我们国家所做的一切都与我的信念背道而驰。

segments.textEn: And I kept this very fond personal friendship with him. And he would allow me on his network and he would require his hosts like Hannity and Neil CAVUTO and Bill O'Reilly to put me on to talk about environmental issues. I was the only environmentalist during those years who was regularly going on Fox News. And in 2016, I had done a documentary on the mercury and vaccines. And I showed it to him and he was very interested.
segments.textZh: 我一直与他保持着非常亲密的私人友谊。他会允许我上他的电视网，还会要求他的主持人，比如汉尼提、尼尔·卡武托和比尔·奥赖利，让我上节目谈论环境问题。那些年里，我是唯一经常上福克斯新闻的环保主义者。2016年，我制作了一部关于汞和疫苗的纪录片。我给他看了，他非常感兴趣。

segments.textEn: And he had a family member who he thought had been injured by a vaccine. And he said, unfortunately, I can't help you with this. He said that any of his hosts who allowed me on TV to talk about this, that he would be forced to fire them. And he said that of his advertising revenues for the nightly news shows were at that point coming from pharma. He told me that on average there is 22 advertisements on a nightly news show and 817 to 18 of those are typically pharmaceutical ads.
segments.textZh: 他有一位家人，他认为那位家人因疫苗而受到了伤害。他说，很遗憾，这件事我帮不了你。他说，他的任何主持人如果允许我上电视谈论这件事，他都会被迫解雇他们。他还说，当时他的晚间新闻节目广告收入来自制药行业。他告诉我，一档晚间新闻节目平均有22条广告，其中通常有817到18条是药品广告。

segments.textEn: And he said if any of his hosts cloud me onto their show without checking with him, he would be forced to fire them. And if he didn't, he would get a call from Rupert. What he said from Rupert within 10 minutes. And of course, he met Rupert Murdoch, who is the owner of Fox News. And that kind of gave me insight to, you know, why nobody on TV wanted to talk about these things. Because, as I said, the pharmaceutical industry not only is dictating, is using those shows, the platform to advertise its product.
segments.textZh: 他说，如果他的任何主持人没有先征求他的同意，就把我云上他们的节目，他都会被迫解雇他们。如果他不这么做，就会接到鲁珀特的电话。他说，是在10分钟内接到鲁珀特的电话。当然，他指的是福克斯新闻的老板鲁珀特·默多克。这让我看清了，你知道，为什么电视上没人愿意谈论这些事情。因为正如我所说，制药行业不仅在发号施令，还利用这些节目、这个平台来为其产品做广告。

segments.textEn: But there's only two countries in the world that allow direct to consumer advertising. One is New Zealand, the other is the United States. And it's largely as a result of that. We take three times the pharmaceutical drugs of any other Western nation. We have the. And we have the worst health outcomes. We pay more for health care than any other nation. And I think we're 79th in the world. We're buying, I think, Mongolia and Cuba and Costa Rica, our health outcomes and.
segments.textZh: 但全世界只有2个国家允许直接面向消费者做广告。一个是新西兰，另一个是美国。很大程度上正是因此，我们服用的药品是任何其他西方国家的3倍。我们的。我们的健康结果也是最差的。我们在医疗保健上的支出比任何其他国家都多。我想我们在全世界排名第79。我们的健康结果，我想，我们买的是蒙古、古巴和哥斯达黎加，还有。

segments.textEn: And pharmaceutical drugs are now the third leading cause of death in our country after cancer and heart dise. And it's not just pharmaceutical companies. I was watching the other day, Good Morning America, and there was an advertisement, I think it was by General Dynamics on Good Morning America. There's nobody in the audience in Good Morning America who is buying killer drones. And so why is General Dynamics advertising on Good Morning America?
segments.textZh: 如今，药品已经成为我国仅次于癌症和心脏疾的第3大死因。而且不只是制药公司。前几天我在看《早安美国》，里面有一则广告，我想是通用动力公司在《早安美国》上投放的。《早安美国》的观众里没有人在购买杀人无人机。那么，通用动力公司为什么要在《早安美国》上做广告？

segments.textEn: Well, of course, they're doing those advertisements because they wanted to dictate the content. They want to be able to have an editorial control over the kind of overton window that Good Morning America is permitted within which discussions on Good Morning America are permitted. So they want to make sure that Americans are enthusiastic about our wars and about a belligerent national policy so that they can continue selling weapons.
segments.textZh: 当然，他们投放那些广告，是因为他们想决定节目内容。他们希望能够对《早安美国》获准处于的那种奥弗顿窗口拥有编辑控制权，也就是《早安美国》上的讨论获准处于的范围。因此，他们想确保美国人热衷于我们的战争和好战的国家政策，这样他们就能继续销售武器。

segments.textEn: And unfortunately, those are the forces that are dictating a lot of the official narrative that we hear from network TV and from the corporate television.
segments.textZh: 遗憾的是，我们从电视网和企业电视台听到的许多官方叙事，正是由这些力量决定的。

segments.textEn: Yeah. In fact, Twitter has seen extreme pressure from advertisers as. And, you know, has at least in the west, seen a advertising boycott from a lot of companies. I would like to for sure thank those companies that have stuck with us, like Apple and Disney and many others. But. But we have in for North America and Europe seen roughly half of our advertising disappear overnight simply because we insist on free speech.

segments.textEn: They give more to lobbying twice with the next biggest industry, more than any other industry. And and President Obama, they could have Obamacare forever. So Obama needed to placate them. And the way that he did it was by making this terrible deal where the federal government could not bargain over the price of pharmaceutical products and Medicare and Obamacare. So Obamacare was going to be create this flood of money to the pharmaceutical industry to buy their products for free, for the patients, for free.
segments.textZh: 他们投入游说的钱是第二大行业的2倍，比任何其他行业都多。而且，而且奥巴马总统，他们可以永远拥有奥巴马医改。所以奥巴马需要安抚他们。他所采取的方式就是达成这项糟糕的交易，让联邦政府无法在联邦医疗保险和奥巴马医改中就药品价格进行谈判。所以奥巴马医改将为制药行业创造这股资金洪流，为患者免费购买他们的产品，免费。

segments.textEn: But we could not bargain like you can in Canada and every other nation. You couldn't bargain with them. So they could charge anything they wanted. And that sealed the deal. And all of a sudden pharma was on the side of it became permissible morally for Democrats to accept money from pharma. And within a year, Democrats were getting more money from pharma than Republicans. And then so that put them on the side of the, you know, pro vaccine side.
segments.textZh: 但我们不能像你在加拿大和其他所有国家那样讨价还价。你不能和他们谈判。所以他们想收多少钱就可以收多少钱。这就敲定了交易。突然之间，制药行业站在了它那一边，民主党人接受制药行业的钱在道德上变得可以接受。不到1年，民主党人从制药行业获得的钱就超过了共和党人。然后，这就让他们站到了那个，你知道，支持疫苗的一边。

segments.textEn: They were kind of, we kind of divided evenly. And then President Trump ran and three times during his presidential campaign, he made the statement that he thought that vaccines were causing autism. And that created this. That issue then became part of the culture war. It became part of the cultural divide. Democrats put that issue into the same anti science dumpster as President Trump's climate denial. And it became now a badge of your party, of your tribe.
segments.textZh: 他们算是，我们算是势均力敌。然后特朗普总统参选了，在他的总统竞选期间，他有3次表示，他认为疫苗正在导致自闭症。这就造成了这种情况。这个议题随后成了文化战争的一部分。它成了文化分裂的一部分。民主党人把这个议题扔进了与特朗普总统否认气候变化相同的反科学垃圾桶。如今，它成了你的政党、你的部落的标志。

segments.textEn: And if you ask questions about vaccines, you were a Trump Republican. And if you, if you had a just a religious belief in their efficacy and safety that could not be questioned, you were a Democrat. And so I watched that, all that play out and watched the Democrats slowly become these pro corporate, pro war, pro censorship Republicans. You know, what had once been Republicans and the Republicans that became Addie's censorship, pro civil liberties, anti war.
segments.textZh: 如果你对疫苗提出疑问，你就是支持特朗普的共和党人。而如果你，如果你只是对它们的效力和安全性抱有一种不容质疑的宗教信仰，你就是民主党人。所以我目睹了这一切的发展，目睹民主党人慢慢变成这些亲企业、亲战争、亲审查的共和党人。你知道，那些过去曾是共和党人的人，而共和党人变成了艾迪的审查、支持公民自由、反战。

segments.textEn: And there's been this tremendous realignment. And I talked more than I wanted to because I really want to hear from Tulsi and hear her take on it.
segments.textZh: 而且发生了这种巨大的重新结盟。我说得比原本想说的更多，因为我真的想听听图尔西的看法，听听她对此的观点。

segments.textEn: Thanks. Thanks, Bobby, and thanks for the question. David, so much of what you said is what drove me to leave the Democratic Party. You know, I wasn't born into a family of Democrats. My parents, frankly, were pretty independent minded people. And so when I first ran for the state House, a seat in the state House of representatives in Hawaii 20 years ago, I had to decide, you know, which party I wanted to join. And as I made that decision, I was inspired by leaders within the Democratic Party, frankly, Bobby, people like your father and your uncle, people like Martin Luther King Jr.
segments.textZh: 谢谢。谢谢你，博比，也谢谢你提出这个问题。戴维，你所说的很多内容正是促使我离开民主党的原因。你知道，我并非出生在一个民主党家庭。坦率地说，我的父母都是思想相当独立的人。所以，当我第一次竞选州众议院，也就是20年前竞选夏威夷州众议院的一个席位时，我必须决定，你知道，我想加入哪个政党。当我作出这个决定时，坦率地说，我受到了民主党内部一些领袖的鼓舞，博比，比如你的父亲和叔叔，还有小马丁·路德·金这样的人。

segments.textEn: Democratic leaders in Hawaii who had gone to the mat for the plantation workers, who were people from Hawaii, people from across Asia, people immigrants from around the world. It was Democratic leaders who came in and fought for their rights to be able to be treated, frankly, like human beings and be set free from the oppressive landowners that were Republican in Hawaii at that time. And so the ideals of, you know, freedom and civil liberties and a big tent, inclusive Democratic Party that welcomed people from all backgrounds and, you know, different ideas was really attractive to me and was, why join the Democratic Party?
segments.textZh: 夏威夷的民主党领袖曾竭尽全力为种植园工人而战，这些工人有来自夏威夷的人、来自亚洲各地的人，还有来自世界各地的移民。是民主党领袖挺身而出，为他们争取能够坦率地说像人一样受到对待的权利，并让他们摆脱当时夏威夷那些共和党地主的压迫。所以，你知道，自由和公民自由的理想，以及一个海纳百川、包容并欢迎各种背景和不同理念人群的民主党，对我真的很有吸引力，也是，为什么加入民主党？

segments.textEn: But fast forward to where we are today, as you said, Bobby. I mean, today's Democratic Party is a party that is under the complete control of this elitist cabal of warmongers. Not only is it being led by warmongers, but we have a situation now where, as we saw last fall, where the Congressional Progressive Caucus, you know, they had the audacity to release a public letter to President Biden very gently, very gently and with a lot of flowery words calling for diplomacy and for him to lead a diplomatic effort to end the war between Russia and Ukraine.
segments.textZh: 但快进到我们今天所处的境地，正如你所说的，博比。我的意思是，今天的民主党是一个完全受这个由战争贩子组成的精英主义小集团控制的政党。它不仅由战争贩子领导，而且我们现在还面临这样一种局面，正如我们去年秋天看到的，国会进步党团，你知道，他们竟敢向拜登总统发布一封公开信，非常温和，非常温和，并用大量华丽的辞藻呼吁开展外交，呼吁他领导一项外交努力，结束俄罗斯与乌克兰之间的战争。

segments.textEn: And within 24 hours, they retracted the letter and essentially were cowering in the corner. You know, we can imagine the kind of pressure that they were under to do that and the kind of public criticism that they received for daring to call for peace. So the voices for peace within the Democratic Party have been silenced. Rather than this big, tense, inclusive Democratic Party, we now have party leaders who are focusing their efforts on dividing us, on racializing every issue, using identity politics to, you know, gain a few political points and votes, undermining fundamental freedoms, freedom of speech, advocating censorship, not only advocating for it, but trying to create government entities in order to shut us up, weaponizing the national security state to go after political opponents.
segments.textZh: 而在24小时内，他们就撤回了这封信，实际上畏缩在角落里。你知道，我们可以想象他们为此承受了怎样的压力，以及他们因为胆敢呼吁和平而受到怎样的公开批评。所以，民主党内部支持和平的声音已经被压制。我们如今拥有的不是这个庞大、紧张、包容的民主党，而是一些把精力集中在分裂我们、把每一个议题种族化、利用身份政治来，你知道，获得一些政治加分和选票、破坏基本自由和言论自由、鼓吹审查的政党领袖；他们不仅鼓吹审查，还试图建立政府机构，以便让我们闭嘴，把国家安全体系武器化来打击政治对手。

segments.textEn: The principles and ideals of the Democratic Party stands for today are directly counter to those that are fundamental and foundational to this country. And now we're at a point where President Biden has most dangerously dragged us essentially to the brink of nuclear war. And that's where. Bobby, I'd love to ask you a question. In this realm, in this vein of foreign policy, given the realities that we are facing, given, you know, we're increasingly hearing a lot of politicians, Republicans and Democrats, frankly, including President Biden, who are actively and aggressively calling for a complete decoupling of the United States and China's economies.
segments.textZh: 民主党如今所代表的原则和理想，与这个国家的根本和奠基原则直接相悖。而现在，我们已经到了拜登总统极其危险地、实质上把我们拖到核战争边缘的地步。而这就是。博比，我很想问你一个问题。在这个领域，在外交政策这个方向上，鉴于我们面临的现实，鉴于，你知道，我们越来越多地听到许多政治人物、共和党人和民主党人，坦率地说也包括拜登总统，正在积极而强硬地呼吁美国与中国的经济彻底脱钩。

segments.textEn: The Biden administration is actively moving forward quickly in this direction. Elon, you recently talked about how the United States and China's interests are intertwined like conjoined twins. I think really making the point that this act of decoupling our economies would essentially be like ripping apart conjoined twins, implying the catastrophic consequences that would occur as a result for both our. Both of These countries and the world.
segments.textZh: 拜登政府正在积极而迅速地朝这个方向推进。埃隆，你最近谈到美国和中国的利益像连体双胞胎一样交织在一起。我认为这实际上是在说明，让我们的经济脱钩这一行为，实质上就像把连体双胞胎硬生生撕开，暗示着由此将给我们双方的。给这2个国家和全世界带来灾难性后果。

segments.textEn: So Bobby, what would your approach be with the United States relationship with China? Do you believe that it's actually possible to have a peaceful coexistence or even a win relationship with China? Or do you believe that it is a zero sum game where in order for the United States to win that China must lose?
segments.textZh: 所以，博比，你会如何处理美国与中国的关系？你是否认为，实际上有可能与中国和平共处，甚至与中国建立一种获胜关系？还是你认为这是一场零和博弈，为了让美国获胜，中国就必须失败？

segments.textEn: Yeah, I think that's a great question, Tulsi. And my, you know, my approach to that would be let's recognize the reality that China is a very ambitious nation and that it does want to compete for us for influence in the world. But the reality is it does not want to, to compete with us militarily. It does not want to have a war with the United States. And China still, you know, is still a very poor country compared to us.
segments.textZh: 是的，我认为这是个很好的问题，图尔西。我的，你知道，我对此的处理方式是，让我们承认这样一个现实：中国是一个雄心勃勃的国家，它确实希望为了争夺在世界上的影响力而与我们竞争。但现实是，它并不想在军事上与我们竞争。它不想与美国开战。而且中国仍然，你知道，与我们相比仍然是一个非常贫穷的国家。

segments.textEn: They have a, the Chinese have per capita about one third the income of the United States. They want to have a better lives for their citizens. And you know, they want to compete with us in places all around the world. I think we ought to be competing, I think we ought to be competing with the, with them on an economic platform, not a military one. And I feel very, I'm not scared of the Chinese. I'm not frightened that American ingenuity is going to fall behind the Chinese.
segments.textZh: 他们的，中国人的人均收入大约是美国的三分之一。他们希望自己的公民过上更好的生活。而且，你知道，他们希望在世界各地与我们竞争。我认为我们应该竞争，我认为我们应该在经济平台上与他们竞争，而不是在军事平台上。而且我非常，我不害怕中国人。我不担心美国人的聪明才智会落后于中国人。

segments.textEn: I think it will be, that kind of competition is a competition that will be good for the whole world. And it's a competition that is a collaborative piece, a collaborative world rather than a competitive world, a kind of collaborative competition, if you will. And you know, the Chinese do not want to have a war with us. We have, we spend more on our military. We're now spending 1.3 trillion a year military, including veterans benefits, which you can't cut back.
segments.textZh: 我认为这将是，那种竞争会是一种对全世界都有益的竞争。而且这是一种具有协作成分的竞争，是一个协作的世界，而不是一个竞争的世界，可以说是一种协作式竞争。而且，你知道，中国人不想与我们开战。我们，我们在军事上的支出更多。我们现在每年在军事上支出1.3万亿，包括不能削减的退伍军人福利。

segments.textEn: But you know, we were told after the Cold War ended that we were going to get a peace dividend and we were going to cut our military budget back to 200 billion a year. Instead we've got it at 1.3 billion a year if you include, you know, veterans and national security and, and we never got that piece dividend. So we now spend more on our militaries in the top 10 next nations in the world. We spend three times, we have three times the military budget of the Chinese.
segments.textZh: 但你知道，冷战结束后，我们被告知将会获得和平红利，并将把军事预算削减到每年2000亿。相反，如果把，你知道，退伍军人和国家安全算在内，我们把它维持在每年13亿，而且，而且我们从未得到那份片段红利。所以，我们现在用于军事的支出超过世界上接下来的前10个国家。我们的支出是3倍，我们的军事预算是中国的3倍。

segments.textEn: The Chinese, we have five times the nuclear weapons of the Chinese. The Chinese cannot and do not want to compete with us militarily. The Chinese have about one and a half military bases in the world. We have 800. So it's kind of a self fulfilling prophecy that says, oh, the Chinese are, you know, want to be our enemy and have a military competition. They don't. What we should be doing is de. Escalating the military pressure on China.
segments.textZh: 中国人，我们拥有的核武器是中国人的5倍。中国人无法、也不想在军事上与我们竞争。中国人在全世界大约有1个半军事基地。我们有800个。所以，这有点像一个自我实现的预言，说，哦，中国人，你知道，想成为我们的敌人，并展开军事竞争。他们不想。我们应该做的是降。低对中国的军事压力。

segments.textEn: We should be talking to China, for God's sake. We haven't had a meeting with China in five years. We know what our objectives are. We want to rebuild our industrial base in the United States. We don't want the Chinese to take that from us. And any negotiations with the Chinese should not be about military swaggering. It should be about how do we have an economic relationship with you that is going to benefit all parties the way that every good economic relationship does.
segments.textZh: 看在上帝的份上，我们应该与中国对话。我们已经5年没有与中国举行会议了。我们知道自己的目标是什么。我们希望重建美国的工业基础。我们不希望中国人从我们手中夺走它。与中国人进行的任何谈判都不应该是军事上的耀武扬威。应该讨论的是，我们如何与你们建立一种能像每一种良好经济关系那样让各方受益的经济关系。

segments.textEn: And here's what our objective is in the next round of negotiations is we want to rebuild our industrial base here in the United States. And any agreement that we make, any transaction that we make with the Chinese, that should be foremost in our minds. How do we do that? But I'm not, you know, the Chinese have been doing a lot better than us because they've been projecting economic power abroad and that the world likes that.
segments.textZh: 而我们下一轮谈判的目标是，我们希望在美国这里重建我们的工业基础。我们达成的任何协议、与中国人进行的任何交易，都应该首先考虑这一点。我们怎么做到这一点？但我并不是，你知道，中国人一直比我们做得好得多，因为他们一直在海外投射经济实力，而世界喜欢这样。

segments.textEn: We think the world is on our side, but it isn't. All we've got. The only people who are supporting this, you know, this pugnacious, bellicose relationship with China are Australia, New Zealand, Korea, Japan, Britain, Canada and the United States. And we're pretty much alone in the world. The rest of the world is looking at us and saying, what the heck are you doing? Why are you trying to create a war with China? Why are you fighting them over.
segments.textZh: 我们以为世界站在我们这边，但事实并非如此。我们所有的。唯一支持这种，你知道，这种与中国好斗、好战关系的人，是澳大利亚、新西兰、韩国、日本、英国、加拿大和美国。而我们在世界上几乎是孤立的。世界其他地方正看着我们说，你们到底在干什么？为什么要试图制造一场与中国的战争？为什么要和他们争夺。

segments.textEn: Over. Why are you making Taiwan a military issue? Let's let Taiwan and China work out that issue on their own and back off militarily and try to have a. They want. They don't want war. They want peace and they want prosperity. And that cannot happen where there's a war. So let's have, you know, let's de. Escalate the war talk. Let's compete economically and let's talk to that and figure out a way that we can have a smart negotiation where we do better because of China rather than giving away the store and exporting jobs, which all the other treaties have done.
segments.textZh: 争夺。为什么要把台湾变成一个军事问题？让台湾和中国自行解决那个问题吧，并在军事上退后，试着拥有一个。他们想要。他们不想要战争。他们想要和平，也想要繁荣。而有战争时，这是不可能实现的。所以，让我们，你知道，让我们缓。和战争言论。让我们在经济上竞争，让我们谈谈这一点，找出一种能够进行明智谈判的办法，让我们因为中国而变得更好，而不是拱手让出一切、把就业岗位输出海外，之前所有其他条约都是这么做的。

segments.textEn: Instead, let's figure out how to have an economic relation, a financial relationship with them that rebuilds the American industrial base.
segments.textZh: 相反，让我们弄清楚如何与他们建立一种经济关系、一种金融关系，从而重建美国的工业基础。

segments.textEn: Thank you, Bobby. This is such an. Obviously, this issue and the broader issue of foreign policy is central to any presidential race. And it's unfortunate that traditionally, as we've seen, these issues are very rarely given the kind of attention they deserve. And yet again, this is exactly why there should be presidential primary debates for the sake of the American people to have a clear choice, a clear, informed choice on who they would like to see as our President and Commander in Chief.
segments.textZh: 谢谢你，鲍比。这是一个如此。显然，这个问题以及更广泛的外交政策问题，是任何一场总统竞选的核心。遗憾的是，正如我们所看到的，传统上这些问题极少得到它们理应获得的那种关注。而且再说一次，这恰恰说明了为什么应该举行总统初选辩论，让美国人民能够明确选择，作出明确、知情的选择，决定他们希望看到谁担任我们的总统兼武装部队总司令。

segments.textEn: Thank you. Thank you for sharing your insight and thank you, Elon and David, for hosting this important conversation.
segments.textZh: 谢谢。感谢你分享见解，也谢谢埃隆和戴维主持这场重要对话。

segments.textEn: And see, you know, we haven't had. We haven't had a serious economic meeting, even a political meeting with the Chinese since 15, seven years. You know, the CIA director, Bill Burns, recently went over there to meet with the Chinese, but that's not the kind of meeting we need to have a real political and economic discussion with them. That is frank and that, you know, that where everybody puts their cards on the table and to see if there's ways that we can work with each other peacefully and keep the world at peace.
segments.textZh: 而且你看，你知道，我们没有过。我们已经没有与中国人举行过严肃的经济会议，甚至政治会议，自15，7年以来。你知道，中央情报局局长比尔·伯恩斯最近去了那里与中国人会面，但那不是我们为了与他们进行真正的政治和经济讨论而需要举行的那种会议。那种讨论应当坦率，而且，你知道，在那里每个人都把自己的牌摊在桌面上，看看我们是否有办法彼此和平合作，并维护世界和平。

segments.textEn: Why in the world would we go and this is on. You know, this is on President. You know, President Biden has forbidden his State Department, which are run by neat, has forbidden any kind of talks or outreach to the Chinese. That is outrageous. You know, it is exactly the opposite of what Dwight Eisenhower was trying to do with, you know, to find a road to peace with the Russians, which was disrupted by the, you know, the CIA misbegotten YouTube flights.
segments.textZh: 我们究竟为什么要去，而这责任在。你知道，这责任在总统。你知道，拜登总统已经禁止他的国务院，而国务院由“整洁”管理，已经禁止与中国人进行任何形式的会谈或接触。这令人愤慨。你知道，这与德怀特·艾森豪威尔当时试图做的事情恰恰相反，他当时试图与，你知道，与俄罗斯人找到一条通往和平的道路，而这被，你知道，中央情报局那些错误的YouTube飞行破坏了。

segments.textEn: And my uncle tried to do the thing, let's have peace with the. With Russia, let's have peace with China, and let's all enjoy the prosperity of healthy economic competition.
segments.textZh: 而我叔叔也试图做这件事，让我们与。与俄罗斯和平相处，让我们与中国和平相处，让我们所有人都享受健康经济竞争带来的繁荣。

segments.textEn: Well said. Well said, Bobby. Thank you.
segments.textZh: 说得好。说得好，鲍比。谢谢。

segments.textEn: It's actually something that is worth. Is that on my recent trip to China, I, with the senior leadership there, I, we had, I think, some very productive discussions on artificial intelligence risks and the need for some oversight or regulation.
